book: What It Takes to Become a Chess Master
author: Andrew Soltis
source: Batsford 2012. The book's nine chapters are nine attributes that separate masters from club players. Each interactive section is an ORIGINAL treatment of one idea — no text is quoted from the book.
audience: Serious club players (~1400–1800) who want to make the leap to master.

chapters.title: What Matters Most
chapters.premise: A master is not smarter and rarely knows more. The edge is three trainable skills: seeing positions as relationships (chunks), scanning forcing moves first, and owning patterns. Above all, a master knows what he wants out of a position and where to steer the game.

spec.goal: Show the difference between how amateurs and masters look at a board: chunks vs piece lists; teach the forcing-moves habit; let the reader play the Fried Liver trap and a full smothered mate.
keyIdeas: Chunks: masters store familiar piece relationships, not 32 pieces
de Groot's five-second tests: master memory is meaning, not images
Checks, captures, threats first — every position, both sides
Patterns are stored calculation: Philidor's legacy (smothered mate)

spec.goal: Teach what Soltis puts at the heart of the book: a master decides early what he wants out of the position and where to steer the game. Every move — even a quiet one — serves that goal. Amateurs move pieces; masters steer positions.
keyIdeas: Name the goal before you move: 'I want the d-file and a knight on e5' beats 'I want to attack'
Steering is slow: small advantages (open file, better bishop, safer king) accumulate
Improve your worst piece — the worst piece is where the next gain is
Quiet moves steer; forcing moves cash in. A master spends most of the game steering
When both players steer, the one with the clearer goal usually lands it
teaching_arc: Open with an amateur trap: wandering moves with no goal vs a master quietly improving
A constructed middlegame position where the reader picks the steering move (quiz: the worst piece's best square or the file seizure), not a tactic — a PLAN move
Show the same position steered well vs steered lazily, two branches
A flash test on a steering position: where will this endgame/rook go?
Close with takeaways tying steering to the skills from 1.1
spec.exerciseMix: 3–4 quizzes whose solutions are strong quiet/steering moves (must still have ONE clearly best answer), at most 1 flash

chapters.title: Habits
chapters.premise: Masters run automatic checks every move: What are his threats? What are my targets? Is my king safe? The habits, not talent, prevent blunders and build initiative — targets equal initiative.

chapters.title: Little Tactics
chapters.premise: Not combinations — the small stuff: little threats, pawn breaks, tempo moves, defensive finesse. Masters win material slowly with moves that barely look like tactics.

chapters.title: More
chapters.premise: Masters know more, and differently: openings they understand rather than memorize, endgame technique, and positions from their own games — knowledge organized for retrieval.

chapters.title: Sense
chapters.premise: Sense of danger: masters feel when a position is about to turn — before the tactic exists. They read the opponent's ideas the way they read their own.

chapters.title: Winnability
chapters.premise: Masters judge which positions are worth fighting for: when to press a drawish position, when a 'won' position is not, and how much fight is left in a position.

chapters.title: Easier
chapters.premise: Making life easier: simplifying when ahead, avoiding counterplay, trading into endings they understand, and steering toward positions that are easy for them and hard for you.

chapters.title: Comp
chapters.premise: Compensation: when material is worth less than the whole. Masters evaluate dynamic sacrifices — attack, structure, time — rather than counting points.

chapters.title: Knowing
chapters.premise: Knowing yourself: your time trouble, your favorite mistakes, the positions you actually win with. Masters build their repertoire and training around who they are at the board.
